unit.unitOverview: This is the largest grammar unit in Level 2 and it fills the biggest gap left by Level 1. The present perfect is the form English uses to connect the past to now, and without it you have to work around any statement about experience, duration or change. Four cards: the form, the two words that measure it, the continuous version, and — last, deliberately — the comparison with the past simple you already have.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns and they build in order.
Open Patterns. Card 4 only compares — do cards 1 to 3 first.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a work history in two formats.
Do the Practice. Practice 4 is the diagnostic for the whole unit.
Record yourself describing experience and change.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This is the biggest thing missing from Level 1, and it is worth knowing why before we start.
In Level 1 you learned the past simple — I worked, I went, I saw. That form puts an event in the past and leaves it there. It is finished, it is separate from now, and usually there is a time attached: I worked there in 2019.
The present perfect does something different. It connects the past to now.
I have worked there. Notice what is missing: any time at all. That sentence is not about 2019. It is about my situation today — I have that experience, it is part of what I am now.
The form. Have or has, plus the past participle.
I have worked. She has worked. They have finished.
The past participle for regular verbs is the same as the past simple — worked, finished, lived. For irregular verbs there is a third form, and you already know many of them: gone, seen, done, been, taken, given, written, spoken. Some are the same as the past: had, made, found, told, left, lost, heard. And a few are different in a way you have to learn: go, went, gone. See, saw, seen. Do, did, done. Take, took, taken.
So the twenty irregulars from Level 1 Unit 14 now need a third column, and for about half of them the third column is the same as the second.
What is the present perfect for? Three jobs.
One: experience at some point in your life, with no particular time. I have worked in three countries. Have you ever been to Italy? I have never eaten it.
Two: something that started in the past and is still true now. I have lived here for six years. That is the job the past simple cannot do at all — I lived here for six years says I do not any more.
Three: a past action with a result you can see now. I have lost my keys, meaning I do not have them at this moment. She has broken her arm, meaning it is broken now.
All three connect back to the present. That is the whole idea, and if you hold it, the rules follow.
Second card: for and since. These measure the connection.
For is followed by a length of time. For six years. For two months. For a long time.
Since is followed by a starting point. Since 2019. Since March. Since I moved here.
The test is simple: if you can answer how long, use for. If you can answer when did it start, use since.
And both of them, with the present perfect, mean the thing is still true. I have lived here since 2019 means I still live here. That is why since almost never appears with the past simple.
Third card: the present perfect continuous. Have been plus the -ing form.
I have been working here for six years. I have been waiting for an hour.
The difference from the plain present perfect is emphasis rather than fact, and this is where most explanations go wrong, so let me be precise.
With a duration, the two are almost interchangeable. I have lived here for six years and I have been living here for six years mean the same thing, and both are correct. Do not agonise over that case.
Where they genuinely differ is in what they focus on. The continuous focuses on the activity itself, and often on it being long, repeated or tiring. I have been waiting for an hour — the waiting is the point, and I am probably not pleased about it. The plain form focuses on the result or the completed quantity. I have written three reports — three is the point. I have been writing reports all day — the writing is the point, and I may not have finished any.
So: how many, use the plain form. How long, and how it felt, use the continuous.
And two verbs that almost never take the continuous, because they describe states rather than activities: know and be. I have known her for ten years, never I have been knowing her.
Fourth card, and I am putting it last on purpose.
The present perfect against the past simple. This is the choice that decides whether the tense sounds natural, and I could not teach it earlier because you did not have the present perfect until ten minutes ago.
The rule is about time, and it is mechanical.
If the sentence has a finished time — yesterday, last year, in 2019, at six o'clock, when I was young — use the past simple. Always. No exceptions worth your attention.
If the sentence has no time, or an unfinished time — today, this week, this year, ever, never, so far, recently — use the present perfect.
I worked there in 2019. Finished time, past simple.
I have worked there. No time, present perfect.
I have worked hard this week. This week is not over, present perfect.
I worked hard last week. Last week is over, past simple.
And the pattern you will hear constantly in real conversation: open with the present perfect, then switch to the past simple for the details.
Have you been to Italy? Yes, I went in 2019. I stayed in Rome for a week and it was extremely hot.
The first question has no time, so it is present perfect. The moment a time appears, everything switches to the past simple and stays there. That two-step is how English actually talks about experience, and if you can produce it you will sound considerably more natural than the grammar alone would suggest.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: The Tense That Connects
readings.passageScript:
The past simple puts an event in the past and leaves it there. I worked in a warehouse in 2019. That sentence is about 2019, and it says nothing about now.
The present perfect connects the past to the present. I have worked in a warehouse. Notice there is no time in that sentence at all, and its absence is the point — it is not about when. It is about what I am now: somebody who has that experience.
The form is have or has plus the past participle. For regular verbs the participle is identical to the past simple, so worked, finished and lived need nothing new. For irregular verbs there is a third form, and the good news is that for roughly half of the common ones it is the same as the past: had, made, found, told, left, lost, heard, kept, sold.
The ones that genuinely need a third form are few and frequent: go went gone, see saw seen, do did done, take took taken, give gave given, write wrote written, speak spoke spoken, be was been.
The present perfect does three jobs, and all three connect back to now.
Experience at no particular time. I have worked in three countries. Have you ever been to Italy?
A situation that started in the past and is still true. I have lived here for six years. The past simple cannot do this at all — I lived here for six years says that I no longer do.
A past action with a present result. I have lost my keys means I do not have them now. She has broken her arm means it is broken now.
That second job is the one worth dwelling on, because it is the gap in Level 1. Without the present perfect, there is no way to say that something began in the past and continues. Learners without it either use the present, which loses the duration, or the past, which wrongly implies it has stopped. Both are understood and both are slightly wrong, and this is why the tense is worth the effort it costs.

readings.title: How Many, or How Long
readings.passageScript:
The present perfect continuous — have been plus -ing — is explained badly more often than almost anything else in English, usually because the explanation implies a sharp difference where there is often none.
So here is the honest version.
With a duration, the two forms are very close and often interchangeable. I have lived here for six years and I have been living here for six years mean the same thing. Both are correct, both are natural, and nobody will notice which you chose. Do not spend effort on this case.
Where they genuinely differ is what they point at.
The plain present perfect points at a result or a completed quantity. I have written three reports. The three is the point. The reports exist.
The continuous points at the activity. I have been writing reports all day. The writing is the point, and it carries an implication the plain form does not: that it has gone on a while, that it may not be finished, and often that the speaker has some feeling about it.
I have been waiting for an hour is not neutral. Nobody says it happily.
So the working rule is: how many, use the plain form. How long, and how it felt, use the continuous.
There is one small group of verbs that resist the continuous entirely, because they describe states rather than activities. Know is the clearest. I have known her for ten years, never I have been knowing her. Be behaves the same way, and so do believe, own and belong.
The test is whether the verb describes something you do or something that is simply true of you. You can be doing waiting. You cannot be doing knowing.
And one thing worth noticing about how the continuous is actually used: it often carries a complaint or an excuse. I have been trying to reach you all week. I have been meaning to do it. Both are doing social work as much as grammatical work.

grammar.title: The present perfect: form and use
grammar.explanation: The form English uses to connect the past to now. This is the largest gap left by Level 1, because without it there is no way to say something started in the past and continues.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FORM:  have / has  +  PAST PARTICIPLE
  I have worked.   She has worked.

THE PARTICIPLE
  regular verbs: same as the past simple
     worked, finished, lived
  half the irregulars: same as the past
     had, made, found, told, left, lost,
     heard, kept, sold
  the ones needing a THIRD form:
     go went gone      see saw seen
     do did done       take took taken
     give gave given   be was been
     write wrote written

THREE JOBS - all connect to NOW

  1  EXPERIENCE, no particular time
       I have worked in three countries.
       Have you ever been to Italy?

  2  STARTED IN THE PAST, STILL TRUE
       I have lived here for six years.
       ^ the past simple CANNOT do this.
         "I lived here for six years"
         means you no longer do.

  3  PAST ACTION, PRESENT RESULT
       I have lost my keys.
       She has broken her arm.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say you have the experience of working in three countries, without saying when.
1. Is there a time in the sentence? No — and that absence is the point.
2. That makes it job one: experience.
3. Build it: have plus the participle. Work is regular, so the participle is worked.
4. Result: I have worked in three countries.
Now job two, which is the gap. You moved here six years ago and you still live here.
1. Started in the past, still true today.
2. The past simple would be wrong: I lived here for six years says you left.
3. Present perfect: I have lived here for six years.
And job three. You cannot find your keys.
1. A past action — losing them — with a result you can see now.
2. I have lost my keys. Notice that the sentence is about the present situation even though the losing happened earlier.
grammar.commonMistake: Using the past simple for a situation that continues — I lived here for six years, when you still live here. It is understood and it says the opposite of what you mean. The other error is the participle: I have went, I have took. Those verbs have a third form and gone and taken are it.
grammar.memoryTip: No time in the sentence, and it connects to now? Present perfect.
grammar.practice:
Write the present perfect.
1. I ____ (work) in three countries.
2. She ____ (live) here for six years.
3. I ____ (lose) my keys.
4. They ____ (go) already.
5. ____ you ever ____ (be) to Italy?
6. He ____ (not finish) it yet.
grammar.answerKey:
1. have worked  2. has lived  3. have lost  4. have gone  5. Have … been  6. has not finished
Numbers 4 and 5 use third forms — gone and been — and both are on the short list worth memorising.
Number 2 is job two, the one the past simple cannot do. If you wrote lived, that sentence would mean she has moved away.
Number 6 puts not between has and the participle, and yet at the end. Both positions are fixed.

grammar.title: For and since
grammar.explanation: The two words that measure the connection to now. One takes a length, the other a starting point, and the test that separates them is a question.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FOR  + a LENGTH of time
  for six years, for two months,
  for a long time, for a decade

SINCE + a STARTING POINT
  since 2019, since March,
  since I moved here, since then

THE TEST
  answers HOW LONG?      -> for
  answers WHEN DID IT START? -> since

BOTH MEAN IT IS STILL TRUE
  I have lived here since 2019.
     = I still live here.

  This is why SINCE almost never appears
  with the past simple. Since points at a
  start that reaches the present, and the
  past simple cuts the connection.

OTHER PARTNERS OF THE PERFECT
  ever, never, already, yet, just,
  so far, up to now, lately, recently,
  this week, this year
grammar.workedExample:
You moved here in 2019 and you still live here. Two ways to say it.
1. If you measure the length: how long? Six years. Length takes for.
   I have lived here for six years.
2. If you name the start: when did it begin? 2019. A starting point takes since.
   I have lived here since 2019.
Both are correct and they say the same thing from two directions.
Now the check that catches errors. Since 2019 is a point on a calendar. For 2019 would be wrong, because 2019 is not a length.
And the reverse: for March is wrong, because March is a starting point, not a length. Since March is right.
When you are unsure, ask the question aloud. How long — for. When did it start — since.
grammar.commonMistake: Swapping them — since six years, for 2019. The test fixes both in one step. The other error is using since with the past simple: I lived here since 2019. Since reaches the present, and the past simple cuts it off, so the two contradict each other in one sentence.
grammar.memoryTip: How long, for. When did it start, since.
grammar.practice:
Write for or since.
1. I have lived here ____ six years.
2. I have lived here ____ 2019.
3. She has worked there ____ March.
4. We have known each other ____ a long time.
5. It has been like that ____ I arrived.
6. He has been waiting ____ an hour.
grammar.answerKey:
1. for  2. since  3. since  4. for  5. since  6. for
The lengths are 1, 4 and 6 — six years, a long time, an hour. The starting points are 2, 3 and 5 — 2019, March, and the moment I arrived.
Number 5 shows that since can take a whole clause, not just a date: since I arrived, since I moved here, since the change.
Every one of these implies the situation is still true. That is not an extra fact — it is what for and since do with the perfect.

grammar.title: The present perfect continuous
grammar.explanation: Have been plus -ing. With a duration it is often interchangeable with the plain form. Where it genuinely differs is what it points at.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FORM:  have / has  been  +  -ING
  I have been working here for six years.

WITH A DURATION - OFTEN THE SAME
  I have lived here for six years.
  I have been living here for six years.
  ^ both correct. Don't agonise here.

WHERE THEY DIFFER - what they POINT AT

  PLAIN -> the RESULT or the QUANTITY
     I have written three reports.
     ^ three is the point.

  CONTINUOUS -> the ACTIVITY
     I have been writing reports all day.
     ^ the writing is the point.
       May not be finished.
       Often carries a feeling.

  "I have been waiting for an hour."
  Nobody says this happily.

THE WORKING RULE
  HOW MANY -> plain
  HOW LONG, and how it felt -> continuous

VERBS THAT RESIST IT
  know, be, believe, own, belong
     I have known her for ten years.
  Test: something you DO, or something
        simply TRUE of you?
grammar.workedExample:
You have produced three reports and you want to say so.
1. What is the point — the activity, or how many? How many.
2. Quantity takes the plain form.
3. Result: I have written three reports.
Now the same day described differently. You want to say you spent all day on reports and may not have finished.
1. The point is the activity and its length.
2. That takes the continuous.
3. Result: I have been writing reports all day.
Notice you have not contradicted yourself. Both can be true of the same day, and they emphasise different things.
Now a verb that resists. You want to say how long you have known somebody.
1. Apply the test: is knowing something you do, or something simply true of you? Simply true.
2. So no continuous: I have known her for ten years.
And the case not to worry about: I have lived here for six years and I have been living here for six years are both fine.
grammar.commonMistake: Using the continuous with a quantity — I have been writing three reports. If a number is present, the plain form is almost always right. The other error is putting a state verb in the continuous: I have been knowing her, I have been being here. The test — do it, or simply true — sorts these without a list.
grammar.memoryTip: How many, plain. How long and how it felt, continuous.
grammar.practice:
Write the plain perfect or the continuous.
1. I ____ (write) three reports today.
2. I ____ (write) reports all day.
3. She ____ (wait) for an hour.
4. We ____ (finish) two of them.
5. I ____ (know) her for ten years.
6. He ____ (try) to reach you all week.
grammar.answerKey:
1. have written — a quantity, so plain
2. have been writing — the activity and its length, so continuous
3. has been waiting — how long, and not happily
4. have finished — a quantity again
5. have known — a state verb; the continuous is impossible here
6. has been trying — the activity, and it carries the implication that he has not succeeded
Numbers 1 and 2 describe the same day and both are true. The difference is what each one points at, not what happened.
Number 6 is doing social work as well as grammar: I have been trying to reach you all week is a complaint, and the plain form would not carry that.

grammar.title: Present perfect versus past simple
grammar.explanation: This card only compares. The past simple is Level 1 Unit 14 and the present perfect is card 1 of this unit — nothing here is new. What is new is choosing, and the choice is decided by the time expression.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
DECIDED BY THE TIME EXPRESSION

  FINISHED TIME -> PAST SIMPLE
     yesterday, last year, in 2019,
     at six, when I was young, ago

  NO TIME / UNFINISHED -> PERFECT
     (none), today, this week, this year,
     ever, never, so far, recently,
     lately, already, yet

  I worked there in 2019.       finished
  I have worked there.          no time
  I have worked hard this week. not over
  I worked hard last week.      over

THE TIME WORD DECIDES, NOT THE SITUATION
  "I qualified in 2018" is past simple
  even though the qualification still
  holds. The date decides it.

THE TWO-STEP YOU WILL HEAR CONSTANTLY
     "Have you been to Italy?"
     "Yes, I went in 2019. I stayed in
      Rome and it was extremely hot."

  One question, then everything switches
  and stays switched.
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody asks whether you have ever been to Italy, and you have.
1. Their question has no time in it, so it is present perfect: Have you been to Italy?
2. Your first word answers that: Yes, I have.
3. Now you add a detail — and the moment you name a year, a finished time has entered the conversation.
4. Everything from that point takes the past simple: I went in 2019. I stayed in Rome for a week. It was extremely hot.
5. Notice you do not switch back.
Now the case that catches people. You qualified in 2018 and the qualification is still valid. Which tense?
1. Reason from the time expression, not from the situation.
2. In 2018 is a finished time.
3. So: I qualified in 2018. Past simple, even though the result still holds.
If you want to say something about the result reaching now, that needs its own sentence: I qualified in 2018 and I have worked in the field ever since.
grammar.commonMistake: Reasoning from the situation instead of from the time word. Learners think the qualification still counts, so the perfect must be right — and the date overrules that. The other error is failing to switch: Have you been to Italy? Yes, I have been in 2019. Once a finished time appears, the past simple takes over.
grammar.memoryTip: Finished time, past simple. No time or unfinished time, present perfect.
grammar.practice:
Choose the tense and say which time word decided it.
1. I ____ (work) there in 2019.
2. I ____ (work) there. (no time given)
3. I ____ (work) hard this week.
4. I ____ (work) hard last week.
5. ____ you ever ____ (be) to Italy?
6. Yes, I ____ (go) in 2019.
grammar.answerKey:
1. worked — in 2019, a finished time
2. have worked — no time at all
3. have worked — this week is not over
4. worked — last week is over
5. Have … been — ever is an unfinished time
6. went — in 2019, a finished time
Numbers 3 and 4 are the clearest pair: the same activity, and the only difference is whether the period has ended.
Numbers 5 and 6 are the two-step. The question has no finished time; the answer supplies one, and the tense switches at that exact point.
